Biosafety of Prion
Diseases
HENRY BARON AND STANLEY B. PRUSINER
INTRODUCTION TO BIOSAFETY ISSUES
Prions are unprecedented transmissible pathogenic
agents that cause a group of invariably fatal neurodegenerative diseases, including scrapie (the prototype prion disease in sheep and goats), bovine
spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) in cattle, chronic
wasting disease (CWD) in deer and elk, and
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) in humans. A complete list of currently known animal and human
prion diseases is provided in Table 1. Prions are unlike any other infectious pathogens,
including viruses, because they are composed of an
abnormal conformational isoform of a normal host
cellular protein, the prion protein (PrP), and are
devoid of a nucleic acid genome. The abnormal isoform, designated PrPSc for “scrapie-like” isoform of
PrP, serves as a template to recruit molecules of
the normal, “cellular” isoform (PrPC), corrupting the
latter to adopt the misfolded conformation of the
former. Prion diseases, therefore, are disorders of
protein conformation involving template-assisted
replication, resulting in PrPSc accumulation in the
brain, which causes neuronal dysfunction, degeneration, and death. This represents a truly novel pathogenetic mechanism. Of the many distinctive features that distinguish
prion diseases from viral, bacterial, fungal, and parasitic disorders, the most remarkable is that prion
diseases can be manifest as infectious, inherited, and
sporadic illnesses. Familial CJD (fCJD), GerstmannStraüssler-Scheinker syndrome (GSS), and fatal
familial insomnia (FFI) are all dominantly inherited
prion diseases linked to mutations in the gene
encoding PrP, whereas sporadic CJD (sCJD) is
thought to be due to a spontaneous conversion of
PrPC to PrPSc.

text:
Familial CJD (fCJD), GerstmannStraüssler-Scheinker syndrome (GSS), and fatal
familial insomnia (FFI) are all dominantly inherited
prion diseases linked to mutations in the gene
encoding PrP, whereas sporadic CJD (sCJD) is
thought to be due to a spontaneous conversion of
PrPC to PrPSc. Yet in all three manifestations of prion
disease, infectious prions are generated in the brains
of afflicted individuals, and these prions are composed of disease-causing PrPSc molecules with the
amino acid sequence encoded by the PrP gene of
the affected host. When prions are passaged into the
brain of a different host species, a “species barrier,”
related primarily to interspecies differences in PrP
sequences and, in some instances, to prion strain, is
responsible for inefficient infection (Pattison, 1965;
Scott et al., 1989; Telling et al., 1995; Scott et al., 1999;
Assante et al., 2002). However, if interspecies transmission does occur, then the prions generated in the
brain of the alternate host carry the amino acid
sequence encoded by the PrP gene of that particular
species, and not the PrP sequence found in the original infectious inoculum. In other words, in interspecies infection, such as from sheep to cattle or
from cattle to humans, the prions that replicate in
the host brain are not the same as those that initiated
replication. This scenario is profoundly different
from what happens during a viral infection. While it

text:
If prion-related risk is evaluated from the
perspective of the virologist, ignoring the unique
properties peculiar to prions, misinformed and
perhaps harmful decisions, based on erroneous
assumptions, could be the consequence. The biosafety issues related to prions have been
addressed in several guidelines published by health
authorities over the years, with recommendations
to limit the potential risk associated with prion contamination in laboratory studies as well as in foods
and medicinal products. These biosafety issues
have taken on a heightened concern over the past
decade, due to the potential transmission of scrapie,
CWD, and, especially, BSE prions to animals and
humans through consumption of contaminated
foodstuffs. Prions in meat and bonemeal (MBM),
most likely derived from scrapied sheep offal, are
believed to be the cause of the BSE epidemic in the
United Kingdom (Wilesmith et al., 1991; Pattison,
1998). The transmission of a similar disease to cats
is suspected to be due to prion-contaminated cat
food (Wyatt et al., 1991). More recently, the demonstration of a link between BSE and a new variant of
CJD (vCJD) (Will et al., 1996; Hill et al., 1997a; Scott
et al., 1999) has provoked a profound reassessment of public health policy worldwide on prionassociated risks to the human population. In
addition, a further potential hazard to human
health was recognized in the administration of biological as well as medicinal products derived from
or associated with human or animal tissues potentially contaminated with prions. Professional, public,
and political reaction to the rising number of CJD
cases in recipients of cadaveric dura mater grafts or
of pituitary-extracted human growth hormone
(HGH) from donor cadavers with undiagnosed CJD
has led to global concerns about potential prion contamination of products derived from human tissues
and about surgical instruments or medical devices
exposed to such tissues.

These concerns have spread
to questions regarding the safety of human blood
and blood products as well. All these fears and anxieties have given rise to a
number of scenarios and forecasts, ranging from the
cavalier to the apocalyptic, with attendant protective
guidelines and measures. In this chapter, we strive
to sort out the truth from the myth and the legitimate from the unreasonable, and provide a factual
basis for concerns as well as an informed rationale
for actions to be implemented. We also explore the
potential consequences of underreaction as well as
overconcern with respect to these issues. BARON AND PRUSINER

BIOSAFETY LEVEL CLASSIFICATION
AND PROFESSIONAL EXPOSURE
Physical Properties of Prions
The smallest infectious prion particle is probably a
dimer or small oligomer of PrPSc. This estimate is
consistent with an ionizing radiation target size of
55  9 kDa (Bellinger-Kawahara et al., 1988).

source: Biological Safety Biosafety of Prion Diseases (Fleming, Diane O. Hunt, Debra L.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk)_removed.pdf
text:
This estimate is
consistent with an ionizing radiation target size of
55  9 kDa (Bellinger-Kawahara et al., 1988). A
recent study designed to evaluate the relationship
between infectivity and the size of PrPSc aggregates
showed that the most infectious prion particles consisted of oligomers of 14 to 28 PrPSc molecules in the
17- to 27-nm (300- to 600-kDa) range (Silveira et al.,
2005). Therefore, prions may not be retained by all
of the filters that efficiently eliminate bacteria and
viruses. Additionally, prions aggregate into particles of nonuniform size that can affect their filtration capacity, and they cannot be solubilized by
detergents, except under denaturing conditions
where infectivity is lost (Gabizon and Prusiner,
1990; Safar et al., 1990). Prions resist inactivation by
nucleases (Bellinger-Kawahara et al., 1987b), UV
irradiation at 254 nm (Alper et al., 1967; BellingerKawahara et al., 1987a), and treatment with psoralens (McKinley et al., 1983), divalent cations,
metal ion chelators, acids (between pH 3 and 7),
hydroxylamine, formalin, boiling, or proteases
(Prusiner, 1982; Brown et al., 1990). Human Prions
Laboratory exposure
Human prions and those propagated in apes and
monkeys are considered biosafety level 2 or 3 pathogens depending on the studies being conducted
(CDC/NIH, 1999). BSE prions are likewise considered biosafety level 2 or 3 pathogens due to the fact
that BSE prions have been transmitted to humans in
the United Kingdom, France, and elsewhere (Will
et al., 1996). All other animal prions are considered biosafety
level 2 pathogens. Thus, based on our current understanding of prion biology described above, once
human prions are passaged in mice and mouse PrPSc
is produced, these prions should be considered
biosafety level 2 prions, although the human prions
are biosafety level 3 under most experimental conditions.

Thus, based on our current understanding of prion biology described above, once
human prions are passaged in mice and mouse PrPSc
is produced, these prions should be considered
biosafety level 2 prions, although the human prions
are biosafety level 3 under most experimental conditions. An exception to this statement concerns mice
expressing human, bovine, or chimeric (human/
mouse or bovine/mouse) transgenes. These animals
produce human, bovine, or artificial prions when
infected with human or animal prions and should be
treated as biosafety level 2 or 3 in accord with the
guidelines described above. Care of patients with human prion disease
In the care of patients dying of human prion disease,
those precautions used for patients with AIDS or hepatitis are certainly adequate. In contrast to these viral
illnesses, the human prion diseases are not contagious (Ridley and Baker, 1993). There is no evidence
of contact or aerosol transmission of prions from one
human to another. However, they are infectious
under some circumstances, such as in the case of ritualistic cannibalism in New Guinea causing kuru, the
administration of prion-contaminated growth hormone causing iatrogenic CJD (iCJD), the transplantation of prion-contaminated dura mater grafts
(Gajdusek, 1977; CDC, 1985, 1997; Public Health
Service Interagency Coordinating Committee, 1997),
and two recent incidents of transfusion-related transmission of vCJD (Llewelyn et al., 2004; Peden et al.,
2004). As stated earlier, fCJD, GSS, and FFI are all
dominantly inherited prion diseases; five different
mutations of the PrP gene have been shown to be
genetically linked to the development of inherited
prion disease. Prions from many cases of inherited
prion disease have been transmitted to apes, monkeys, and mice carrying human or chimeric PrP transgenes (Brown et al., 1994a; Telling et al., 1995; Telling
et al., 1996; Korth et al., 2003).

Prions from many cases of inherited
prion disease have been transmitted to apes, monkeys, and mice carrying human or chimeric PrP transgenes (Brown et al., 1994a; Telling et al., 1995; Telling
et al., 1996; Korth et al., 2003). Surgical procedures, including brain biopsy
Surgical procedures on patients with a diagnosis of
prion disease should be minimized. It is thought
that CJD has been spread from a CJD patient who
underwent neurosurgical procedures to two other
patients shortly thereafter in the same operating
theater (Brown et al., 1992). Although there is no documentation of the transmission of prions to humans
through contact with droplets of blood or cerebrospinal fluid or by exposure to intact skin or gastric
and mucous membranes, the risk of such occurrences
cannot be ruled out. Sterilization of the instruments
and the operating room should be performed in
accord with recommendations described below and
in chapter 20 of this book. Because it is important to establish a definitive
diagnosis of a human prion disease and to distinguish between sporadic or familial cases and those
acquired by infection as a result of medical procedures or from prion-contaminated food products,
unfixed brain tissue should be obtained. For all
cases of suspected human prion disease, a minimum of 1 cm3 of unfixed cerebral cortex should be
part of any biopsy sample. This specimen should
be bisected from the cortical surface through to the
underlying white matter, with one half of the specimen formalin fixed and the other half frozen. 26. BIOSAFETY OF PRION DISEASES

Autopsy procedure
Routine autopsies and the processing of small
amounts of formalin-fixed tissues containing human
prions require biosafety level 2 precautions. At
autopsy, the entire brain is collected and cut into
coronal sections about 1.5 in. (4 cm) thick; small
blocks of tissue can be removed easily from each
coronal section and placed in fixative for subsequent
histopathologic analyses. Each coronal section is
immediately heat sealed in a heavy-duty plastic bag. The outside of this bag is assumed to be contaminated with prions and other pathogens. With fresh
gloves or with the help of an assistant with uncontaminated gloves, the bag containing the specimen
is placed into another plastic bag, which does not
have a contaminated outer surface. The samples are
then frozen on dry ice or placed directly in a 70C
freezer for storage. At the very minimum, a coronal
section of cerebral hemisphere containing the thalamus and one of the cerebellar hemispheres and
brain stem should be taken and frozen. The absence of any known effective treatment for
prion disease demands caution in the manipulation
of potentially infectious tissues. The highest concentrations of prions are in the central nervous system
(CNS) and its coverings. Based on data from animal
studies, it is possible that high concentrations of prions may also be found in spleen, thymus, and lymph
nodes. Moreover, in vCJD, prions are routinely
detected in lymphoid tissue of tonsil, spleen, and
appendix (Hill et al., 1997b; Bruce et al., 2001;
Wadsworth et al., 2001; Hilton et al., 2004). In addition, prion infectivity and/or PrPSc has been found in
muscle tissue of experimentally infected mice
(Bosque et al., 2002) and patients who died of sCJD
(Glatzel et al., 2003).

In addition, prion infectivity and/or PrPSc has been found in
muscle tissue of experimentally infected mice
(Bosque et al., 2002) and patients who died of sCJD
(Glatzel et al., 2003). The main precaution to be taken
when working with prion-infected or -contaminated
material is to avoid puncture of the skin (Ridley and
Baker, 1993). The prosector should wear cut-resistant
gloves if possible. If accidental contamination of skin
occurs, the area is swabbed with 1 N sodium hydroxide for 5 min and then washed with copious amounts
of water. Tables 2 to 5 provide guidelines to reduce
the chance of skin punctures, contamination from
aerosols, and contamination of operating room and
morgue surfaces and instruments. Further information on prion disinfection approaches, including
waste management and decontamination, is provided below and in chapter 20 of this book. Unfixed
samples of brain, spinal cord, and other tissues containing human prions should be processed with
extreme care at biosafety level 3. Animal Prions

TABLE 2
Autopsies of patients with suspected prion disease: Standard Precautions
1. Attendance is limited to three staff, including at least one experienced pathologist. One of the staff avoids direct
contact with the deceased but assists with handling of instruments and specimen containers. 2. Standard autopsy attire is mandatory. However, a disposable, waterproof gown is worn in place of a cloth gown. a. Cut-resistant gloves are worn underneath two pairs of surgical gloves, or chain mail gloves are worn between
two pairs of surgical gloves. b. Aerosols are created mainly during opening of the skull with a Stryker saw, requiring the use of personal protective equipment during this phase of the autopsy.

two pairs of surgical gloves. b. Aerosols are created mainly during opening of the skull with a Stryker saw, requiring the use of personal protective equipment during this phase of the autopsy. At the University of California, San Francisco, the approved
system for protection from aerosols is an AIR-MATE HEPA 12 powered air-purifying respiratory system
(RACAL Health and Safety, Inc., Frederick, Md.). This unit consists of the following parts:
i. Polycoated Tyvek head cover
ii. HEPA filter unit containing battery pack, belt, and HEPA filter
iii. AC adapter/charger
iv. Airflow indicator
v. Breathing tube assembly
c. The above respirator system can be worn throughout the autopsy; however, when no aerosols are being generated, such as when the brain is being removed or when organ samples are being removed in situ, the staff may
switch to a surgical mask with a wraparound splash guard transparent visor. 3. To reduce contamination of the autopsy suite
a. The autopsy table is covered with an absorbent sheet that has a waterproof backing. b. Contaminated instruments are placed on an absorbent pad. c. The brain is removed with the head in a plastic bag to reduce aerosolization. d. The brain can be placed into a container with a plastic bag liner for weighing. e. The brain is placed onto a cutting board and appropriate samples are dissected for snap-freezing (see Table 3). f. The brain or organs to be fixed are immediately placed into a container with 10% neutral buffered formalin. g. In most cases of suspected prion disease, the autopsy can be limited to examination of the brain only.

Laplanche et al., 1999), as do the risk and number of
sheep potentially infected with BSE prions (Kao
et al., 2002). Epidemiological studies have been conducted on the potential risk of transmission of
scrapie prions to humans but have never supported
a causal relationship (Chatelain et al., 1981). Thus,
scrapie prions are considered biosafety level 2
pathogens. BSE
As stated earlier, BSE prions are considered to have
been transmitted to humans through oral consumption of contaminated beef. Therefore, the risk of
infection for humans by BSE prions by the oral
route is established. The most prudent approach to
prevent laboratory exposure and contamination is
to study BSE prions in a biosafety level 2 or 3 facility, depending on the studies to be performed as
noted above for human prions. Other “naturally” occurring animal prion
diseases
CWD in mule deer and elk, transmissible mink
encephalopathy (TME), feline spongiform encephalopathy (FSE), and exotic ungulate encephalopathy
(EUE) are all thought to occur after the consumption of prion-infected foods (Gajdusek, 1991; Marsh,
1992; Collinge and Palmer, 1997; Prusiner, 1997).

text:
Other “naturally” occurring animal prion
diseases
CWD in mule deer and elk, transmissible mink
encephalopathy (TME), feline spongiform encephalopathy (FSE), and exotic ungulate encephalopathy
(EUE) are all thought to occur after the consumption of prion-infected foods (Gajdusek, 1991; Marsh,
1992; Collinge and Palmer, 1997; Prusiner, 1997). Despite anecdotal observations of CJD in people
who were either deer hunters or consumers of venison (Belay et al., 2004) and in a man whose pet cat
had contracted FSE (Zanusso et al., 1998), there is
currently no evidence of any risk to humans posed
by the above-mentioned animal prion diseases,
though more epidemiological and laboratory data
are needed to monitor the possibility of such transmissions. Therefore, these prions are considered
biosafety level 2 pathogens. Experimental rodent prion diseases
Mice and hamsters are the experimental animals of
choice for all studies of prion disease. With the development of transgenic mice that are highly susceptible
to human prions, the use of apes and monkeys is no
longer justified, except for certain well-designed
pathogenesis studies. The highest titers of prions
(109 50% infectious doses [ID50]/g) are found in the
brain and spinal cord of laboratory rodents infected
with adapted strains of prions (Eklund et al., 1967;
Prusiner et al., 1980); lower titers (106 ID50/g) are
present in the spleen and lymphoreticular system
(Kimberlin, 1976; Prusiner et al., 1978). As with other
animal prions (except for BSE prions), experimental
rodent prions are considered biosafety level 2
pathogens. 26. BIOSAFETY OF PRION DISEASES

TABLE 3
Autopsy suite decontamination procedures
1. Instruments (open box locks and jaws) and saw blades are placed into a large stainless steel dish, soaked for 1 h in
2 N sodium hydroxidea or for 2 h in 1 N sodium hydroxide, and/or autoclaved at 134C (gravity displacement
steam autoclaving for 1 h; porous load steam autoclaving for one 18-min cycle at 30 lb in2 or six 3-min cycles at
30 lb in2). 2. The Stryker saw is cleaned by repeated wiping with 2 N sodium hydroxide solution. 3. The absorbent table cover and instrument pads, disposable clothing, etc., are double bagged in appropriate
infectious waste bags for incineration. 4. Any suspected areas of contamination of the autopsy table or room are decontaminated by repeated wetting over
1 h with 2 N sodium hydroxide. aA 5% sodium hypochlorite solution with at least 20,000 ppm of free chloride for 2 h, or 96% formic acid may substitute but will
corrode the stainless steel. TABLE 4
Brain-cutting procedures
1. After adequate formaldehyde fixation (at least 10–14 days), the brain is examined and cut on a table covered with
an absorbent pad with an impermeable backing. 2. Samples for histology are placed in cassettes labeled with “CJD Precautions.” For laboratories that do not have
embedding and staining equipment or a microtome dedicated to infectious diseases, including CJD, blocks of
formalin-fixed tissue can be placed in 95–100% formic acid for 1 h, followed by fresh 10% neutral buffered formalin
solution for at least 48 h (Brown et al., 1990). The tissue block is then embedded in paraffin as usual.

Inactivation of prions
Prion infectivity is diminished by prolonged digestion with proteases and other treatments such as boiling in sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS). Sterilization of
rodent brain extracts with high titers of prions
requires autoclaving at 132C for 4.5 h, denaturing
organic solvents such as phenol (1:1), chaotropic
agents such as guanidine isocyanate or hydrochloride
(4 M), or alkali such as NaOH for 24 h (Prusiner
et al., 1984; Prusiner et al., 1993; Taylor et al., 1995;
Taylor et al., 1997). With the exceptions noted above, biosafety level 2
practices and facilities are recommended for all activities utilizing known or potentially infectious tissues
and fluids containing nonhuman prions from naturally or experimentally infected animals. Although
there is no evidence to suggest that aerosol transmission occurs in the natural disease, it is prudent to
avoid the generation of aerosols or droplets during
the manipulation of tissues or fluids and during the
necropsy of experimental animals. It is further
strongly recommended that gloves be worn for activities that provide the opportunity for skin contact
with infectious tissues and fluids. Formaldehydefixed and paraffin-embedded tissues, especially of
the brain, remain infectious.

It is further
strongly recommended that gloves be worn for activities that provide the opportunity for skin contact
with infectious tissues and fluids. Formaldehydefixed and paraffin-embedded tissues, especially of
the brain, remain infectious. Some investigators recommend that formalin-fixed tissues from suspected
cases of prion disease be immersed for 30 min in 96%
formic acid or phenol before histopathologic processing (Brown et al., 1990), but such treatment may distort the microscopic neuropathology and/or alter
some immunohistochemical reactions. Prions are characterized by extreme resistance to
conventional inactivation procedures, including irradiation, boiling, dry heat, and chemicals (formalin,
-propiolactone, and alcohols). However, they are
inactivated by 1 N NaOH, 4.0 M guanidinium
hydrochloride or isocyanate, sodium hypochlorite
(2% free chlorine), and steam autoclaving at 132C
for 4.5 h (Prusiner et al., 1984; Prusiner et al., 1993;
Taylor et al., 1995; Taylor et al., 1997). It is recommended that dry waste be autoclaved at 132C for
4.5 h or incinerated. Large volumes of infectious liquid waste containing high titers of prions can be completely sterilized by treatment with 1 N NaOH (final
concentration) followed by autoclaving at 132C for
4.5 h. Disposable plasticware, which can be discarded
as a dry waste, is highly recommended. Because the
paraformaldehyde vaporization procedure does not
diminish prion titers, the biosafety hoods must be
decontaminated with 1 N NaOH, followed by 1 N
HCl, and rinsed with water; HEPA filters should be
autoclaved and incinerated. Recent fears of the potential spread of human
prion disease, particularly vCJD, through contaminated surgical instruments, as well as other medical
and dental equipment, prompted investigators to
research novel, less corrosive methods for prion disinfection. Some of these consisted of modifications
of conventional cleaning reagents which were
reported to have utility in diminishing prion titers
(Fichet et al., 2004; Race and Raymond, 2004).

Some of these consisted of modifications
of conventional cleaning reagents which were
reported to have utility in diminishing prion titers
(Fichet et al., 2004; Race and Raymond, 2004). A recent major breakthrough, however, was reported
in an investigation of the inactivation of prions by
SDS in weak acid (Peretz et al., 2006). Using SDS
combined with autoclaving for 15 min completely
inactivated sCJD prions bound to stainless steel
wires, providing the basis for a noncorrosive system
suitable for inactivating prions on surgical instruments and other medical and dental equipment. BARON AND PRUSINER
TABLE 5
Tissue preparation
1. Histology technicians should wear gloves, an apron, a laboratory coat, and eye protection. 2. Adequate fixation of small tissue samples (e.g., biopsy samples) from a patient with suspected prion disease is
followed by postfixation in 96–100% formic acid for 1 h, followed by 48 h in fresh 10% formalin (see Table 4). 3. Liquid waste is collected in a 4-liter waste bottle containing 600 ml of 6 N sodium hydroxide and diluted to a final

HUMAN-TO-HUMAN TRANSMISSION
OF PRIONS
Infectious Human Prion Disease
Kuru
The story of kuru merits constant retelling. It shows
how the study of a rare, obscure disease affecting a
primitive population in a remote part of the world
could have a profound impact on biomedical science by helping unlock the door to the discovery of
a fascinating, unprecedented infectious agent and
mechanism of disease. Kuru was the first of the
human prion diseases to be shown to be infectious. The demonstration of its transmissibility was
achieved by passaging the disease to chimpanzees
by Gajdusek and his coworkers in 1966 (Gajdusek
et al., 1966), though the neuropathologic similarities
between kuru and the sheep disease known as
scrapie had been established years earlier by
Hadlow (Hadlow, 1959), who set forth the hypothesis that kuru, like scrapie, was a “slow virus” disease, and proposed the primate transmission
experiments that Gajdusek ultimately performed. Kuru, a fatal neurodegenerative disorder restricted
to the Fore population of the mountainous highlands
of Papua New Guinea (Gajdusek and Zigas, 1957),
is now extinct.

text:
Kuru, a fatal neurodegenerative disorder restricted
to the Fore population of the mountainous highlands
of Papua New Guinea (Gajdusek and Zigas, 1957),
is now extinct. But at its peak in the early 1960s, it
caused more than half of all deaths in the affected
population (Alpers, 1987). One of the key observations which elucidated the mode of transmission of
kuru was its unusual epidemiological pattern
(Alpers, 1987). It affected primarily women and
their children of both sexes (Fig. 1). This pattern was
consistent with the predominant role of women and
children in the practice of ritualistic endocannibalism, in which the women and their children consumed parts of the cadavers, including the brain
and viscera, of deceased relatives as an affirmation
of respect. Since the cessation of cannibalism in the
late 1950s/early 1960s, the incidence of kuru has
progressively declined to the point of extinction
(Fig. 1). It is interesting, however, that cases of kuru
continued to appear but at a very low rate until only
a few years ago; yet in all of these recent cases there
was a history of participation in cannibalistic rites
during childhood. This observation provides
insight into the potentially very long incubation
periods of infectious human prion diseases, which
in the case of kuru have been shown to range from
4.5 to 40 years. 26. BIOSAFETY OF PRION DISEASES

iCJD
Since the extinction of kuru, all currently known
cases of infectious, human-to-human transmission
of prions are iCJD. iCJD accounts for less than 1% of
total CJD worldwide. Until the recent observation
of infection of two transfusion recipients who
received packed red cells donated by individuals
who, 18 to 36 months after their donations, developed vCJD (Llewelyn et al., 2004; Peden et al., 2004),
iatrogenic human prion disease had always
involved transmission of prions originating from
the CNS, where there is potential for high levels of
infectivity, or from tissues intimately associated
with the CNS, such as the cornea, pituitary gland,
and dura mater (Brown et al., 1992). The current status of these forms of iCJD, with
respect to source of contamination, numbers of
cases, and mode of transmission, is summarized in
Table 6. New cases continue to appear, particularly
in relation to administration of HGH extracted from
cadaver pituitary glands in France (roughly 60% of
the total cases identified worldwide thus far), and
to dura mater transplantation in Japan, where more
than 80 cases have been reported. An intriguing susceptibility factor associated
with iCJD appears to involve a polymorphism at
codon 129 of the PrP gene. In the Caucasian population, three amino acid phenotypes have been identified at this codon: heterozygous methionine/valine
(Met/Val) in approximately half of all subjects
tested, homozygous Met/Met in roughly 40%, and
homozygous Val/Val in about 10% (Owen et al.,
1990; Collinge et al., 1991; Laplanche, 1996).

In the Caucasian population, three amino acid phenotypes have been identified at this codon: heterozygous methionine/valine
(Met/Val) in approximately half of all subjects
tested, homozygous Met/Met in roughly 40%, and
homozygous Val/Val in about 10% (Owen et al.,
1990; Collinge et al., 1991; Laplanche, 1996). In iCJD,
however, only about 10% of all studied cases are
heterozygous Met/Val, with an overrepresentation
of homozygous Met/Met (60%) and Val/Val
(30%), suggesting that homozygosity at this site
may predispose an individual to the acquisition of
disease following exposure to exogenous human
prions (Collinge et al., 1991; Brown et al., 1994a;
Deslys et al., 1996; Deslys et al., 1998; Laplanche,
1996). In sCJD, there is an even greater overrepresentation of homozygous Met/Met (80%), with a
representative proportion of Val/Val (10%) but an
underrepresentation of heterozygous Met/Val
(10%) (Palmer et al., 1991; Laplanche, 1996; Parchi
et al., 1996). Whether these differences at codon 129
truly predispose to heightened susceptibility to
acquired CJD, or whether they simply modulate the
duration of the incubation period, remains to be
determined. The situation bears close watching,
however, particularly in France, where recent cases
of HGH-related iCJD in Met/Val heterozygotes
could be of ominous portent (Deslys et al., 1998). If
heterozygosity at codon 129 is not truly protective
but only confers prolonged incubation periods, an
already dramatic situation in France could represent only a fraction of the total number of cases. Risk of prion transmission through human blood
and blood products

human by blood transfusion or through administration of blood components or plasma derivatives has
long been a cause for concern among health professionals throughout the world.

Risk of prion transmission through human blood
and blood products
The potential transmission of prions from human to
human by blood transfusion or through administration of blood components or plasma derivatives has
long been a cause for concern among health professionals throughout the world. In the previous edition
of this book, it was stated that there was no confirmed example of the transmission of prions from a
human blood donor who later developed CJD to a
recipient (Baron and Prusiner, 2000), though several
investigators had suggested that such transmissions
were possible (Manuelidis, 1994; Brown, 1995;
Ricketts et al., 1997). This statement can still be made
concerning the sporadic, inherited, and iatrogenic
forms of CJD, which make up the vast majority of
cases of human prion disease. However, it can no
longer be made with assurance regarding vCJD
(Llewelyn et al., 2004; Peden et al., 2004). If a recipient of a blood transfusion, blood components, or plasma derivatives develops CJD, the critical question is whether this is a case of iCJD
transmitted through blood or blood products or of
sCJD, which occurs worldwide at an incidence of 1
case per million population per year. The difficulty
comes in distinguishing iCJD from sCJD. In both

cases, wild-type PrPSc is found in the brains of the
patients, which is a unique feature of prion disease. If
CJD were caused by a virus, then the virus isolated
from the blood or blood product that was given to
the patient could be compared to that recovered from
the patient. In prion diseases, only PrPSc from the
CJD donor can be compared to that recovered from
the recipient CJD patient, but the detection of PrPSc in
blood from a CJD patient has not yet been reliably
accomplished. Such an approach may prove feasible
in the future with the use of highly susceptible transgenic mice expressing human PrP and/or highly sensitive conformation-dependent immunoassays (CDIs). The application of transgenic mice and CDIs to the
field of prion biology is so new that many “applied
studies” have not yet been completed. Previous
investigations with nontransgenic rodents have often
not employed experimental designs utilizing adequate controls and safeguards against potential contamination. Such controls are essential in the study of
prion diseases because of the extraordinary resistance
of prions to standard decontamination procedures. Experimental Data
Prion infectivity in blood or blood constituents has
been reported in multiple studies with experimentally infected laboratory rodents (Clarke and Haig,
1967; Dickinson and Fraser, 1969; Manuelidis et al.,
1978; Kuroda et al., 1983; Diringer, 1984; Casaccia
et al., 1989). However, these studies must be considered in the context of their experimental designs, in
which the animals were inoculated with exogenous
prions, either peripherally or intracerebrally, and
part of the inoculum probably found its way across
disrupted blood vessels into the bloodstream during the inoculation procedure.

However, these studies must be considered in the context of their experimental designs, in
which the animals were inoculated with exogenous
prions, either peripherally or intracerebrally, and
part of the inoculum probably found its way across
disrupted blood vessels into the bloodstream during the inoculation procedure. Infectivity levels in
these rodent blood samples, as estimated by the
incubation periods in bioassay animals, were 102
ID50 per ml, compared to 106 to 107 ID50 per g of
brain tissue (Brown, 1995). More recent studies have shown that blood components and plasma of wild-type mice intracerebrally inoculated with mouse prions contain prion
infectivity in buffy coat and plasma primarily during the clinical stage of disease, but at very low levels: 100 infectious units (IU) per ml for buffy coat
and 20 IU/ml for plasma (Brown et al., 1998;
Brown et al., 1999; Brown et al., 2001). These data
suggest that in these experimental models, infectivity in blood is primarily associated with the leukocyte fraction. While the application of information obtained
from different experimental rodent models to the
human situation is interesting, it must be stressed
that in the vast majority of CJD cases, i.e., sCJD and
fCJD, which account for more than 99% of the total
number of CJD cases worldwide, no penetrating
inoculation event occurs as in experimental prion
disease in laboratory animals. Moreover, it is now
believed that both sCJD and fCJD result from a
spontaneous conversion of PrPC into PrPSc. This
being the case, it can be argued that there is no reason to suspect passage of infective material into the
bloodstream in these forms of human prion disease,
except possibly in late stages of disease when there
is breakdown of the blood-brain barrier.

being the case, it can be argued that there is no reason to suspect passage of infective material into the
bloodstream in these forms of human prion disease,
except possibly in late stages of disease when there
is breakdown of the blood-brain barrier. iCJD, which
represents less than 1% of total CJD and for which
inoculation of exogenous prions via injection or surgical procedure is documented, may pose a greater
potential risk of blood-borne prions. Current blood
donor selection criteria as discussed below exclude
most donors at risk for iCJD. In a series of experimental studies designed to
explore the potential transmissibility of vCJD from
human to human via transfusion, sheep were used
as a model to evaluate cross-species transmission of
cattle-derived BSE prions by the oral route and then
intraspecies transmission from these orally challenged sheep by transfusion (Hunter et al., 2002). The investigators reported transmission of prion
disease in 2 of 24 sheep transfused with blood from
sheep orally challenged with BSE prions, as well as
in 4 of 21 sheep transfused with blood drawn from
sheep with natural scrapie. Questionable study
design and perplexing incubation time data, not
allowing determination or even estimation of titers
of infectivity in blood that transmitted disease, render interpretation of these studies difficult. Moreover,
they are still ongoing and the data are evolving, so
more clarification may emerge as this work progresses. Nonetheless, these results provided a warning that asymptomatic vCJD blood donors could
pose a risk to the blood supply. To this date, there have been no systematic, wellcontrolled studies of the potential for transmission of
human prions from blood of CJD patients using
highly susceptible assay animals that exhibit no
species barrier.

from buffy coats of Alzheimer’s disease patients and

as suggested by one or more of the following
problems: incubation times in animals inoculated
with blood and urine (Tateishi, 1985) and plasma
(Tamai et al., 1992) comparable to those in animals
inoculated with brain from the same patient,
irreproducibility in a subsequent experiment
(Brown, 1995; Doi, 1991 [regarding Tateishi, 1985]),
very long incubation periods (all), and very high
unexplained mortality in both inoculated and control groups (Deslys et al., 1994). In contrast to these anecdotal, putatively positive
but controversial isolations of prion infectivity from
human blood using relatively unsusceptible rodent
hosts presenting significant species barriers, data
obtained from studies using more susceptible nonhuman primates have been uniformly negative. Attempts at the NIH to transmit disease from the

routes of inoculation were all unsuccessful (Brown

buffy coats of patients with vCJD using two different methodologies: bioassay in wild-type mice

In conclusion, a review of the published experimental data did not unearth an abundance of evidence to support the perception that human blood
may contain prions. Of course, this does not mean
that the notion of prion infectivity in human blood
can be dismissed, but only that it is not supported by
any of the foregoing transmission studies, many of
which have been flawed. Moreover, it is now highly
probable that asymptomatic carriers of vCJD prions
who were blood donors transmitted disease to transfusion recipients (Llewelyn et al., 2004; Peden et al.,
2004). The consistent detection of prions in rodent
lymphoid tissues (Eklund et al., 1967; Dickinson and
Fraser, 1969; Lavelle et al., 1972; Kimberlin, 1976;
Prusiner et al., 1978; Kitamoto et al., 1991; Muramoto
et al., 1993; O’Rourke et al., 1994; Brown et al., 1996;
Fraser et al., 1996; Klein et al., 1997) and in lymphoid
tissues of patients with vCJD (Hill et al., 1997b; Bruce
et al., 2001; Wadsworth et al., 2001; Hilton et al., 2004)
gives cause to suspect the presence of prions in blood
carried by circulating lymphocytes during some
phase of the illness. However, the relevance of such
findings in experimentally inoculated rodents to CJD
in humans remains unclear. In any event, the apparent difficulty in demonstrating prions in human
blood argues that if they are present, they must exist
at very low concentrations. At present, we have no knowledge of the titers
and distribution of prions in human blood or extraneural tissues. Moreover, we currently have no
means of identifying asymptomatic individuals who
are destined to develop CJD. Without such diagnostic tools, even the detection and measurement of prions in blood of symptomatic patients with CJD are
problematic.

text:
Moreover, we currently have no
means of identifying asymptomatic individuals who
are destined to develop CJD. Without such diagnostic tools, even the detection and measurement of prions in blood of symptomatic patients with CJD are
problematic. We describe these problems not to paint
a hopeless picture but to delineate where additional
research needs to focus in order to gain urgently
needed information. The application of highly sensitive prion detection technologies such as bioassay in
transgenic mice (Telling et al., 1995; Telling et al.,
1996; Scott et al., 1999; Korth et al., 2003) and the CDI
(Bellon et al., 2003; Safar et al., 2005) to attempt to
resolve these important public health issues appears
to be crucial. Recent results with the CDI adapted to
a “sandwich” format using a capture monoclonal
antibody specific to human PrP show extremely high
sensitivity for human prions (Bellon et al., 2003), surpassing sensitivity levels obtained by bioassay in
transgenic mice (Safar et al., 2005). Epidemiological Data
Until 2 years ago, when vCJD was reported to have
been transmitted from a blood donor in an asymptomatic incubation phase to a transfusion recipient
(Llewelyn et al., 2004), available epidemiological
data did not suggest prion contamination of blood,
blood components, or plasma derivatives. In fact,
these data still argue against transmission of the
classical forms of CJD through blood. Before dealing separately with vCJD and its implications for
the safety of blood products later in this chapter, we
first shall discuss the epidemiological data regarding classical CJD and blood. Epidemiological analysis of this issue is based on
five different types of studies: (i) case reports,
(ii) case control studies, (iii) routine surveillance,
(iv) cohort investigation of recipients from CJD
donors, and (v) special population studies.

Epidemiological analysis of this issue is based on
five different types of studies: (i) case reports,
(ii) case control studies, (iii) routine surveillance,
(iv) cohort investigation of recipients from CJD
donors, and (v) special population studies. A survey of case reports attempting to link CJD to
blood transfusion or administration of blood products failed to reveal any convincing instances of
prion transmission via blood. The utility of case
reports in identifying causative links between CJD
cases and therapeutic products or devices should
not be underestimated, since case reports provided
the initial warnings of the implications of HGH
treatment (CDC, 1985) and dura mater grafts (CDC,
1989, 1997; Prichard et al., 1987) in CJD transmission. Case control studies of CJD conducted in the
United States (Davanipour et al., 1985), the United
Kingdom (Esmonde et al., 1993), Europe (van Duijn
et al., 1998), Australia (Collins et al., 1999), and
Japan (Kondo and Kuroiwa, 1982) have addressed
the issue of whether receiving blood is a risk factor
for CJD. In all of these investigations, there is no
evidence of a higher proportion of CJD cases having
a history of blood transfusion than that of control
subjects. More recent, unpublished, ongoing case
control studies in the United States (CDC, 1996;
L. B. Schonberger, personal communication) and
the United Kingdom (R. G. Will, personal communication) continue to show that blood exposure is
not a risk factor for CJD. There are no significant
differences between CJD and control populations
with respect to receiving or donating blood. Routine surveillance studies of the epidemiology
of CJD have been conducted in many countries and
even repeated in some (Brown et al., 1987; Holman
et al., 1995; Will, 1996; Ruffie et al., 1997; Nakamura
et al., 1999).

Routine surveillance studies of the epidemiology
of CJD have been conducted in many countries and
even repeated in some (Brown et al., 1987; Holman
et al., 1995; Will, 1996; Ruffie et al., 1997; Nakamura
et al., 1999). With the exception of the United
Kingdom, where vCJD has altered the traditional
epidemiological pattern of CJD, the disease continues to have a similar and constant incidence (approximately 1 case per million population per year) and
age distribution (peak in the 60s to 70s, rare under
30), despite increasing use of blood transfusion and
plasma proteins. Perhaps the most compelling evidence against
transmission of CJD through blood or blood products

In studies from the CDC, no patients afflicted with
hemophilia A, hemophilia B, -thalassemia, or sickle
cell anemia have contracted CJD in the United States
over a 17-year period (L. B. Schonberger, personal
communication). Since clotting factor concentrates
for hemophiliacs can come from pools of 20,000 to
30,000 donors, hemophiliacs should have been
exposed to prions if they were present in blood at
appreciable levels. The CDC currently is actively
seeking cases of CJD in hemophiliacs; yet, they have
seen no evidence of CJD in the hemophilia community despite increased surveillance since 1994 (Evatt
et al., 1998). In another CDC study of 101 patients
who received over 238,000 units of cryoprecipitate
over a 17-year period, no cases of CJD were found. Moreover, 76 of these cryoprecipitate users were still
alive a minimum of 12 years later, and 3 had received
at least one unit from a known CJD donor. Finally, the CJD surveillance unit in Edinburgh,
Scotland, conducted a retrospective review of the
postmortem brains of 33 hemophilia patients who
were treated with clotting factor concentrate of predominantly United Kingdom donor sources during
the years 1962 to 1995 (Lee et al., 1998). No evidence
of CJD was found in any of these cases. In conclusion, the data from epidemiological
studies conducted in several parts of the world converge toward the argument that classical CJD prions are not transmitted from human to human
through blood or blood derivatives. While it has
been stated that epidemiological methods are limited in the detection of rare events such as CJD
(Ricketts et al., 1997), the multiple studies currently
underway in many countries should continue to
give additional information about the risk of transmitting the classical forms of CJD through blood or
blood products. Regarding vCJD, as explored
below, the situation is substantially different.

text:
Regarding vCJD, as explored
below, the situation is substantially different. Regulatory Policies
The prevailing view among regulatory authorities
with respect to the risk of transmitting CJD or vCJD
prions through blood and blood products is that not
enough is known about the potential of individuals
in a preclinical, asymptomatic phase to carry infectious prions in their blood. Thus, in the absence of a
specific and sensitive diagnostic test, it is assumed
that such “carriers” might disseminate infection by
blood donation while escaping identification until
the onset of symptoms and signs of CJD. Therefore,
regulatory groups have adopted the position that
transmission of CJD/vCJD through blood constitutes a possible risk and that appropriate measures
must be taken to preclude the occurrence of bloodrelated CJD/vCJD in the future. Their actions
toward that objective are reflected in a series of documents issued by the Committee for Propietary
Medicinal Products (CPMP) and Committee for
Human Medicinal Products (CHMP) of the European Medicines Evaluation Agency (EMEA) and by
the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. These
include the requirement of screening from the blood
donor population all individuals considered theoretically at risk of carrying infectious prions, essentially those at risk for inherited CJD (family history
of neurodegenerative disease), iCJD (history of having received cadaver pituitary-extracted HGH or a
dura mater graft), or CJD (anyone who spent a
defined cumulative period of time in the United
Kingdom, France, and other European countries
reporting BSE and/or vCJD) (CPMP, 1998 and
1999a; CHMP, 2004a; FDA, 1999 and 2002). In addition, investigation of separation and fractionation procedures for removal or carryover of
prion infectivity has been encouraged (CPMP,
1999b; CHMP, 2004a, 2004b; FDA, 2002).

prion infectivity has been encouraged (CPMP,
1999b; CHMP, 2004a, 2004b; FDA, 2002). Such studies are designed to address two essential questions
with respect to the prion safety of blood and particularly plasma-derived products: where does prion
infectivity segregate during fractionation, and what
clearance factor or safety margin is achieved in fractionation? Two recent European regulatory documents propose an algorithm for assessment of prion
removal in manufacturing processes for plasma
derivatives (CHMP, 2004a) and a set of guidelines as
to the design and conduct of these studies (CHMP,

Because infectious prions have never been
detected in or isolated from human blood or plasma,
the design of these prion reduction/removal investigations is problematic in several aspects: first is the
choice of the prion itself (strain or species origin?),
second is the choice of the tissue from which it is
derived (brain, spleen, or other?), and third is the
choice of the prion preparation (brain homogenate,
microsomes, or purified PrPSc?). Since prions do not
behave as ideal particles in either crude or highly
purified preparations, and since there is no knowledge as to the physicochemical properties of the
infectious prion in blood, the choice of an appropriate inoculum as spiking agent intended to mimic the
prion contaminant in blood or plasma is difficult. Other issues include the selection of appropriate
detection methodologies for measuring the concentrations of prions in different compartments or fractions. Is laboratory animal bioassay using rodent
brain-derived prion strains and wild-type rodents
(mice or hamsters) as assay animals an appropriate
model system, or should human CJD/vCJD prions
and transgenic mice expressing human PrP be used?

and transgenic mice expressing human PrP be used? Or can in vitro cell culture systems or immunoassays for PrPSc be employed in these studies? Because many of these questions remain unanswered, persisting uncertainties continue to challenge the design of these prion removal evaluations,
and consensus has not been achieved on many of
these issues. Nonetheless, considerable progress has
been made in recent years in several laboratories
using different approaches and methodologies
(Brown et al., 1998; Brown et al., 1999; Brown et al.,
2001; Lee et al., 2001; Stenland et al., 2002; Vey et al.,
2002; Foster, 2004). In effect, despite the use of different spiking agents and prion detection methodologies, the data all seem to converge to indicate that the
manufacturing processes for plasma-derived medicinal products would reduce prion infectivity considerably if it were present in human plasma. In our opinion, microsomal preparations derived
from brain or lymphoid tissues from transgenic mice
expressing human PrP on the null (Prnp0/0, i.e., mice
which are homozygous for ablation of the endogenous mouse PrP gene referred to as Prnp) background may provide an excellent, renewable source
of relevant, titered inocula for spiking experiments. Such prions can be readily bioassayed in mice
expressing chimeric human/mouse PrP transgenes
(Telling et al., 1994, Telling et al., 1995; Telling et al.,
1996; Korth et al., 2003). Moreover, new highly sensitive immunoassays can be used for many aspects
of these studies (Safar et al., 1998; Safar et al., 2005). Regulatory policy with respect to required actions
upon discovery of a blood donor who subsequently
develops CJD or vCJD has undergone continuous
review and revision over the years.

Moreover, new highly sensitive immunoassays can be used for many aspects
of these studies (Safar et al., 1998; Safar et al., 2005). Regulatory policy with respect to required actions
upon discovery of a blood donor who subsequently
develops CJD or vCJD has undergone continuous
review and revision over the years. In the United
States, following a special FDA advisory committee
meeting in 1995, the FDA decided to withdraw all
lots of any blood or plasma product emanating from
a single donation or from a pool involving a donor
who was diagnosed with CJD after giving blood. The
same year, EMEA’s CPMP in Europe ruled against
withdrawal, considering CJD a rare disease and the
risk of transmission via blood products purely theoretical. However, France in 1996 and Italy in 1997
decided to break with the CPMP position, ruling to
assess each potential withdrawal situation on a caseby-case basis. Japan decided to adopt the U.S. policy
in 1997, ruling in favor of withdrawal. The CPMP
modified its own position in 1998, when it ruled to
withdraw plasma-derived medicinal products if a
donor to a plasma pool was subsequently diagnosed
as having vCJD, at the same time reaffirming its position that withdrawal is not justified in the case of an
sCJD or fCJD donor (CPMP, 1998). Today, these regulatory policies have become relatively harmonized
across most countries. Retrieval and quarantine of all
blood components and recovered plasma emanating
from a donor who was diagnosed with CJD or vCJD
after giving blood are required on a global basis
(FDA, 2002; CPHP, 2004a).

Today, these regulatory policies have become relatively harmonized
across most countries. Retrieval and quarantine of all
blood components and recovered plasma emanating
from a donor who was diagnosed with CJD or vCJD
after giving blood are required on a global basis
(FDA, 2002; CPHP, 2004a). Withdrawal is not considered justified in the case of plasma-derived products
from pooled-source plasma involving an sCJD or
fCJD donor, due to the overwhelming absence of epidemiological evidence of transmission of these forms
of CJD via blood products and to evidence of prion
removal capacity of plasma protein manufacturing
processes as described above. Such withdrawal is
required, however, when a vCJD donor is implicated
in a plasma pool for reasons described below. Regulatory requirements diverge somewhat with
respect to donor exclusion criteria. Although United
Kingdom residence is generally considered a risk
factor, there is some discordance with respect to
duration and time period spent in the United
Kingdom, and policies differ regarding potential
donors who resided in European countries other
than the United Kingdom (FDA, 2002; CHMP,
2004a). Geography-based donor deferral requirements are also less widespread for plasma derivatives than for blood components, due to the robust
prion removal capacity demonstrated for many
manufacturing steps, as described above (FDA,
2002; CHMP, 2004a). In conclusion, the possible risk of humanto-human prion transmission through blood is
under continuing review by worldwide regulatory
authorities. Efforts have been made to ensure the
safety of the blood supply and of plasma derivatives

To
what extent these measures can be successful in
reducing this risk is unclear. Country-based exclusion policies are largely inefficient, as the vast majority of excluded donors will not develop vCJD. Also,
a potential consequence could be shortages of blood
components, as well as a lack of spare plasma capacity to make up for the shortfalls that such measures
might provoke (FDA, 2002; CHMP, 2004a). The
closely intertwined issues of safety and availability must always be considered in terms of a risk/
benefit scenario when applying the precautionary
principle. To prevent compromising the supply of
life-enhancing and life-sustaining blood, blood components, and plasma derivatives requires judicious
evaluation of risk as well as an ongoing reassessment of new information as it becomes available. ANIMAL-TO-HUMAN TRANSMISSION
OF PRIONS
BSE and vCJD—Transmission of Bovine Prions
to Humans and Subsequent Human-to-Human
Transmission
BSE is the most worrisome of all the animal prion
diseases from a biosafety standpoint. It is widely
thought to be a man-made epidemic, caused by a
form of industrial cannibalism in which cattle were
fed MBM produced through faulty industrial
processes from prion-contaminated cattle and sheep
offal (Wilesmith et al., 1991; Anderson et al., 1996;
Prusiner, 1997; Pattison, 1998). Epidemiologically,
BSE has shown a disquieting propensity to cross
species barriers through oral consumption of prioncontaminated bovine foodstuffs (Kirkwood et al.,
1990; Wyatt et al., 1991; Willoughby et al., 1992), and
this propensity has been confirmed experimentally
in laboratory transmission studies employing several routes of inoculation, including the oral and
intravenous routes (Barlow and Middleton, 1990;
Dawson et al., 1990; Fraser et al., 1992; Baker et al.,
1993; Foster et al., 1996; Lasmézas et al., 1996;
Lasmézas et al., 2001; Hunter et al., 2002).

source: Biological Safety Biosafety of Prion Diseases (Fleming, Diane O. Hunt, Debra L.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk)_removed.pdf
text:
Most
alarmingly, there is now solid epidemiological and
experimental evidence that BSE is responsible for
vCJD primarily in the United Kingdom but also elsewhere (Collinge et al., 1996; Lasmézas et al., 1996;
Will et al., 1996; Bruce et al., 1997; Hill et al., 1997a;
Zeidler et al., 1997; Scott et al., 1999). The importance of vCJD with respect to biosafety
is that it represents the first example of transmission
of animal prions to humans (Knight, 1999). Once
kuru was experimentally transmitted to apes
(Gajdusek et al., 1966), the search for an animal reservoir intensified but none was found. Eventually, ritualistic cannibalism became accepted as the mode of
kuru transmission (Gajdusek, 1977). The transmission of sCJD to apes (Gibbs et al.,
1968) stimulated a 25-year search for a relationship
between scrapie in sheep and CJD in humans, but
none was identified. Exhaustive epidemiological
studies were conducted in the hope of identifying
scrapie prions as the cause of CJD (Malmgren et al.,
1979; Will and Matthews, 1984; Brown et al., 1987;
Cousens et al., 1990). When vCJD was first reported,
the differences in one or more of the seven amino
acids that distinguish bovine from sheep PrP were
hypothesized at the time to be the reason that
bovine, but not sheep, prions may have been transmitted to humans. Subsequently, the BSE strain of
bovine prions also was offered as the most important factor in their permissivity in humans (Scott
et al., 1999). It is now clearly established that vCJD is due to
the transmission of bovine prions to humans.

source: Biological Safety Biosafety of Prion Diseases (Fleming, Diane O. Hunt, Debra L.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk)_removed.pdf
text:
Subsequently, the BSE strain of
bovine prions also was offered as the most important factor in their permissivity in humans (Scott
et al., 1999). It is now clearly established that vCJD is due to
the transmission of bovine prions to humans. This
conclusion is based on multiple lines of inquiry:
(i) the spatial-temporal clustering of vCJD (Will et al.,
1996; Zeidler et al., 1997); (ii) the successful transmission of BSE to macaques, with induction of PrP
plaques similar to those seen in vCJD (Lasmézas
et al., 1996); (iii) the similarity of the glycosylation
pattern of the disease-related isoform of PrP in vCJD
to that noted in mice, domestic cats, and macaques
infected with BSE prions (Collinge et al., 1996);
(iv) experimental BSE transmission studies in mice
which suggest that vCJD and BSE behave as the
same prion strain (Bruce et al., 1997); and (v) conclusive studies in transgenic mice expressing bovine
but not mouse PrP which are equally susceptible to
infection with BSE and vCJD prions, showing identical strain-related characteristics, such as clinical
and neuropathologic findings, molecular properties
of pathogenic PrP isoforms, and duration of incubation periods with both inocula (Scott et al., 1999;
Scott et al., 2005). In contrast, the same transgenic
mice injected with sheep scrapie prions also come
down with disease but with markedly different
strain characteristics. These data argue unequivocally that BSE and vCJD are the same prion strain
and remove virtually any doubt that vCJD is a direct
result of consumption of products from BSE-infected
cattle. Yet, a number of enigmas still surround vCJD and
require an adequate explanation. Why should the
disease strike young people predominantly, with a
majority in their teens and twenties?

1997b; Bruce et al., 2001; Wadsworth et al., 2001;
Hilton et al., 1998; Hilton et al., 2004) which raised

acquired and not a sporadic illness, it was reasonable
to assume a hematogenous phase at some point in
the evolution of the disease, raising troubling questions regarding transfusion practice, due to uncertainties surrounding the number of blood donors
who could be incubating and ultimately develop
vCJD (Turner, 1999). This troubling prospect became
an alarmingly high probability when it was reported
in the United Kingdom that a transfusion recipient
developed vCJD about 6 years after transfusion
(Llewelyn et al., 2004). The donor had developed
vCJD roughly 3 years after the identified donation. While it cannot be ruled out definitively that the
transfusion recipient, like the donor, could have contracted vCJD by eating BSE-contaminated beef products, statistical analysis concluded this possibility to
be extremely remote. A second putative transfusion
transmission was reported several months later
(Peden et al., 2004). In this instance, the recipient died
of causes unrelated to vCJD 5 years after receiving a
transfusion from a donor who developed vCJD a little more than a year after the identified donation. At
autopsy, there was no evidence of vCJD pathology or
pathogenic PrPSc in the brain of the recipient, but
PrPSc was revealed to be present in the recipient’s
spleen and lymph nodes. It is difficult to interpret the
significance of the second incident of a vCJD donorrecipient link, but it raised the spectre of possible
vCJD infection in lymphoid tissue of clinically
asymptomatic individuals.

been incorporated into various risk assessments on
potential vCJD transmission by whole blood and
blood components for transfusion as well as by

positions on the risk of vCJD transmission through
blood components and plasma derivatives, advocating precautionary withdrawal, donor deferral measures, and investigation of manufacturing processes
for prion reduction capacity, appear to be a prudent
response. Risk of Prion Transmission through Foodstuffs
and Therapeutic Products Derived from or
Associated with Bovine Source Materials
Against this backdrop, considerable concern has
erupted in Europe over the safety not only of foodstuffs but also of pharmaceutical and biological
products either derived from bovine source materials (active ingredients) or manufactured with
bovine raw materials used as reagents in production. Additionally, there is concern about products
that contain bovine components as excipients in
final formulations or as constituents in the ingested
product covering (capsule material).

The specified offals bans instituted in the United
Kingdom in 1988 and 1989 were based largely on data
derived from studies using Swiss mice for the bioassay of sheep prions. The legislation made two
assumptions: (i) the distribution of prions in cattle
with BSE is the same as that in sheep with scrapie,
and (ii) bioassays of non-CNS sheep prions in mice
yielded reliable data. While we are unaware of any
comparative study of the distribution of prions in
sheep and cattle, there are studies that allow for a
comparison of prion titers in mice and Syrian hamsters. Such quantitative data show clear differences
between these rodent hosts (Kimberlin and Walker,
1977). Equally disturbing is the bioassay of tissues
with low titers in nontransgenic mice. Typically,
Swiss mice require an incubation time of 500 days
before showing signs of scrapie when inoculated with
a 1% brain homogenate from a sheep with scrapie
(Hadlow et al., 1982). Greatly prolonged incubation
times have also been recorded for BSE prions with a
variety of mouse strains (Fraser et al., 1992; Bruce
et al., 1997; Lasmézas et al., 1997). Moreover, the titer
of BSE prions in bovine brain measured by endpoint
titrations in cattle in an ongoing neuropathogenesis
study (Wells et al., 1998) is more than 1,000-fold

Since the beginning of 2000,
testing of bovine brain stems has been mandated in
all E.U. member countries for cattle over 30 months
of age, resulting in the detection of thousands of
cases of BSE in apparently normal cows at the
slaughterhouse. However, the sensitivity reported
for most of these tests is at best comparable to the relatively inefficient wild-type (RIII) mouse bioassay
described above (Moynagh et al., 1999). In a study
designed to calibrate the CDI to infectivity measurements in transgenic mice, the CDI was shown to be
capable of detecting PrPSc in bovine brain stems with
a sensitivity similar to that of endpoint titrations in
Tg(BoPrP)Prnp0/0 mice, which have been shown to
be 10-fold more sensitive than cattle and thus
10,000-fold more sensitive than RIII mice (Safar
et al., 2002). It is clear that the use of immunoassays
considerably less sensitive than the CDI has already
been instrumental in detecting PrPSc in the brain
stems of several thousand asymptomatic cattle at
slaughterhouses in Europe. How many more would
have been found or may be found in the future using
the CDI, which is now approved by the EC for
screening bovine brain stems, is of considerable
interest and may have important implications for the
safety of the food supply. While USDA surveys of “highest risk cattle” have
failed to reveal any cases of BSE in the United States
as noted above, this surveillance is far too limited
and is not directed toward identifying asymptomatic cases. Moreover, the recent limited application
of relatively low-sensitivity immunoassays for PrPSc
has already detected the first two cases of BSE in
asymptomatic cows.

Moreover, the recent limited application
of relatively low-sensitivity immunoassays for PrPSc
has already detected the first two cases of BSE in
asymptomatic cows. In Germany, which now
reports roughly 400 cases of BSE, only a tiny minority occurred in cattle that exhibited overt signs of
clinical disease; the vast majority were detected in
asymptomatic animals at slaughterhouses by
immunoassay (Office International des Epizooties
[http://www.oie.int]). It is also notable that a TME
outbreak in Stettsonville, Wis., in 1985 is thought to
have been due to a sporadic case of BSE in a “fallen
cow” (Marsh et al., 1991). Since the incubation
period for BSE is 3 to 4 years, most infected cattle
will never show neurologic deficits because the vast
majority of cattle in the United States are slaughtered by 1 year of age. Such animals might harbor
significant titers of prions but not show any signs of
CNS dysfunction, histologic evidence of spongiform
degeneration, or immunohistochemical demonstration of PrPSc. We argue that the availability of highly
sensitive methods for detection of PrPSc in brain
stems and other tissues of cattle ought to be
employed routinely in slaughterhouses not only in
the United States but also worldwide to ensure that
humans are not infected by bovine prions. As has
been performed for the CDI, calibration of the sensitivity of such methods by bioassay in Tg(BoPrP)
Prnp0/0 mice should be mandatory. The overemphasis given to BSE in this chapter is
not intended to underestimate the potential
biosafety concerns related to some of the other animal prion diseases, particularly scrapie in sheep and
CWD in deer and elk. Scrapie has been known for
over 200 years, and the bulk of evidence over time,
as stated earlier, does not support the notion that the
scrapie prion is a human pathogen.

Scrapie has been known for
over 200 years, and the bulk of evidence over time,
as stated earlier, does not support the notion that the
scrapie prion is a human pathogen. CWD is more
recent, first described in the 1960s, and first determined to be a prion disease around 1980 (Williams
and Young, 1980). Its growing numbers and everexpanding geographical distribution in recent years
have caused considerable concern. There appears to
be no evidence to date that CWD has been transmitted to humans, despite incidents in which individuals who consumed wild game and/or were hunters
developed CJD (Belay et al., 2004). In addition, in
vitro conversion studies in which normal PrP is
bound to PrPSc show evidence of a molecular species
barrier inhibiting conversion of human, cattle, and
sheep PrP when put in contact with PrPSc prepared
from brain of a deer with CWD (Raymond et al.,
2000). Nonetheless, despite this lack of evidence of
pathogenicity of scrapie or CWD prions to humans,
surveillance and testing for these diseases are crucial
to limiting their future prevalence and spread, and
to ensuring the safety of the food supply against prions regardless of their species origin or strain. To this effect, the reported ability of the CDI to detect
PrPSc from CWD-infected animals with high sensitivity and to discriminate PrPSc from CWD and BSE
prions represents a major advance (Safar et al.,
2002). CONCLUSIONS ON THE BIOSAFETY
OF PRIONS
From this review of some of the biosafety issues
related to prions, whether transmitted cattle to
human via BSE-contaminated bovine products or
human to human through vCJD-contaminated blood,
it becomes readily apparent that existing knowledge
is still incomplete. This situation squeezes regulatory
authorities into the uncomfortable position of having
to recommend highly conservative precautionary
measures aimed at precluding possible risk.

The history of prions is a fascinating saga in the annals of biomedical science. For nearly five decades with no clue as to the cause, physicians
watched patients with a central nervous system (CNS) degeneration
called Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) die, often within a few months of
its onset (Creutzfeldt 1920; Jakob 1921; Kirschbaum 1968). CJD
destroys the brain while the body remains unaware of this process. No
febrile response, no leucocytosis or pleocytosis, and no humoral immune
response is mounted in reaction to this devastating disease. Despite its
recognition as a distinct clinical entity, CJD remained a rare disease; first,
it was the province of neuropsychiatrists and, later, neurologists and neuropathologists. Although multiple cases of CJD were recognized in families quite early (Kirschbaum 1924; Meggendorfer 1930; Stender 1930;
Davison and Rabiner 1940; Jacob et al. 1950; Friede and DeJong 1964;
Rosenthal et al. 1976; Masters et al. 1979, 1981a,b), this observation did
little to advance understanding of the disorder. The unraveling of the etiology of CJD is a wonderful story that has
many threads, each representing a distinct piece of the puzzle. An important observation was made by Igor Klatzo in 1959, when he recognized
that the neuropathology of kuru resembled that of CJD (Klatzo et al.
1959); the same year, William Hadlow suggested that kuru, a disease of
New Guinea highlanders, was similar to scrapie, a hypothesis also based
on light microscopic similarities (Hadlow 1959).

However, Hadlow’s
insight was much more profound because he suggested that kuru is a
transmissible disease like scrapie and that demonstration of the infectivity
of kuru could be accomplished using chimpanzees because they are so

S.B. Prusiner
closely related to humans. He also noted that many months or years might
be required before clinically recognizable disease would be seen in these
inoculated nonhuman primates. Moreover, he argued that brain tissue from
patients dying of kuru should be homogenized and injected intra-cerebrally into the chimpanzees, as was often done in studies of sheep scrapie. At the time Hadlow’s hypothesis was set forth, scrapie was considered
to be caused by a “slow virus.” The term “slow virus” had been coined by
Bjorn Sigurdsson in 1954 based on his studies in Iceland on scrapie and
visna of sheep (Sigurdsson 1954). Although Hadlow suggested that kuru,
like scrapie, was caused by a slow virus, he did not perform the experiments required to demonstrate this phenomenon (Hadlow 1959, 1995). In
fact, seven years were to pass before the transmissibility of kuru was
established by passaging the disease to chimpanzees (Gajdusek et al.
1966), and in 1968, the transmission of CJD to chimpanzees after intracerebral inoculation was reported (Gibbs et al. 1968). An early clue to unusual properties of the scrapie agent emerged from
studies of 18,000 sheep that were inadvertently inoculated with the scrapie
agent or “slow virus.” These animals had been vaccinated against louping
ill virus with a formalin-treated suspension of ovine brain and spleen that,
as was subsequently shown, had been contaminated with the scrapie agent
(Gordon 1946). Three different batches of vaccines were administered, and
two years later, 1500 sheep developed scrapie.

Three different batches of vaccines were administered, and
two years later, 1500 sheep developed scrapie. These findings demonstrated that the scrapie agent is resistant to inactivation by formalin, unlike
most viruses, which are readily inactivated by such treatment. The unusual biological properties of the scrapie agent were no less
puzzling than the disease process itself, for the infectious agent caused a
devastating degeneration of the CNS in the absence of an inflammatory
response (Zlotnik 1962; Beck et al. 1964). Although the immune system
remained intact, its surveillance system was unaware of a raging infection. The infectious agent that causes scrapie, now generally referred to as
a “prion,” achieved status as a scientific curiosity when its extreme resistance to ionizing and ultraviolet irradiation was discovered (Alper et al.
1966, 1967; Latarjet et al. 1970). Later, similar resistance to inactivation
by UV and ionizing radiation was reported for the CJD agent (Gibbs et al.
1978). Tikvah Alper’s radiation resistance data on the scrapie agent
evoked a torrent of hypotheses concerning its composition. Suggestions
as to the nature of the scrapie agent ranged from small DNA viruses to
membrane fragments to polysaccharides to proteins, the last of which
eventually proved to be correct (Pattison 1965; Gibbons and Hunter 1967;
Griffith 1967; Pattison and Jones 1967; Hunter et al. 1968; Field et al.
1969; Hunter 1972; see Chapter 2). Introduction 3
Because the scrapie agent had been passaged from sheep into mice
(Chandler 1961), scrapie was the most amenable of these diseases to
study experimentally. Although the agents causing scrapie, CJD, and kuru
were for many years thought to be different slow viruses, we now know
that prions cause all these disorders and that this distinction was artificial.

Although the agents causing scrapie, CJD, and kuru
were for many years thought to be different slow viruses, we now know
that prions cause all these disorders and that this distinction was artificial. Studies of prions have wide implications ranging from basic principles
of protein conformation to the development of effective therapies for
prion diseases (Prusiner 1998). In this chapter, the structural biology of
prion proteins, as well as the genetics and molecular neurology of prion
diseases, is introduced. How information is enciphered within the infectious prion particle is described. PRION BIOLOGY AND DISEASES
Our current understanding of the prion particles that cause scrapie, CJD,
and related diseases in mammals is described in this book (Table 1). Prions are unprecedented infectious pathogens that cause a group of
invariably fatal, neurodegenerative diseases by an entirely novel mechanism (Prusiner 1998). Prion diseases may present as genetic, infectious,
or sporadic disorders, all of which involve modification of the prion protein (PrP). CJD generally presents as a progressive dementia whereas
scrapie of sheep and bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) are generally manifest as ataxic illnesses (Wells et al. 1987). Prions have also been reported in yeast and other fungi. These fascinating studies have greatly expanded our thinking about the role of prions
in biology (Chapter 6). Prions
Prions are defined as proteinaceous infectious particles that are devoid of
nucleic acid and seem to be composed exclusively of a modified isoform
of the prion protein designated PrPSc (Table 2). The normal, cellular PrP
denoted PrPC is converted into PrPSc through a process whereby some of
its α-helical structure is converted into β-sheet (Pan et al. 1993). This
structural transition is accompanied by profound changes in the physicochemical properties of the PrP.

The normal, cellular PrP
denoted PrPC is converted into PrPSc through a process whereby some of
its α-helical structure is converted into β-sheet (Pan et al. 1993). This
structural transition is accompanied by profound changes in the physicochemical properties of the PrP. Whereas PrPC is soluble in nondenaturing
detergents, PrPSc is not (Meyer et al. 1986; Chapter 5). PrPC is readily
digested by proteases whereas PrPSc is partially resistant (Oesch et al.
1985). The species of a particular prion is determined by the sequence of
the chromosomal PrP gene of the mammal in which it last replicated. S.B. Prusiner
Human PrP is encoded by a gene on the short arm of chromosome 20, and
all other mammals examined also have a single-copy gene encoding PrP
(Sparkes et al. 1986; Schätzl et al. 1995). In contrast to pathogens with a
nucleic acid genome, prions encipher strain-specific properties in the tertiary structure of PrPSc. Transgenetic studies argue that PrPSc acts as a
template upon which PrPC is refolded into a nascent PrPSc molecule and
that this process is facilitated by another protein or complex of proteins. Although both the primary structure and posttranslational chemical
modifications determine the tertiary structure of PrPC, the conformation
of PrPC is modified by PrPSc as it is refolded into a nascent molecule of
